title: Arbitrators, Mediators, and Conciliators
description: Facilitate negotiation and conflict resolution through dialogue. Resolve conflicts outside of the court system by mutual consent of parties involved.
tasks: Prepare written opinions or decisions regarding cases.
Apply relevant laws, regulations, policies, or precedents to reach conclusions.
Conduct hearings to obtain information or evidence relative to disposition of claims.
Determine extent of liability according to evidence, laws, or administrative or judicial precedents.
Rule on exceptions, motions, or admissibility of evidence.
Confer with disputants to clarify issues, identify underlying concerns, and develop an understanding of their respective needs and interests.
Use mediation techniques to facilitate communication between disputants, to further parties' understanding of different perspectives, and to guide parties toward mutual agreement.
Conduct initial meetings with disputants to outline the arbitration process, settle procedural matters, such as fees, or determine details, such as witness numbers or time requirements.
Evaluate information from documents, such as claim applications, birth or death certificates, or physician or employer records.
Research laws, regulations, policies, or precedent decisions to prepare for hearings.
Issue subpoenas or administer oaths to prepare for formal hearings.
Set up appointments for parties to meet for mediation.
Recommend acceptance or rejection of compromise settlement offers.
Prepare settlement agreements for disputants to sign.
Authorize payment of valid claims.
Interview claimants, agents, or witnesses to obtain information about disputed issues.
Conduct studies of appeals procedures to ensure adherence to legal requirements or to facilitate disposition of cases.
Specialize in the negotiation and resolution of environmental conflicts involving issues such as natural resource allocation or regional development planning.
Organize or deliver public presentations about mediation to organizations, such as community agencies or schools.
Participate in court proceedings.

psychological_profile.core_drive: To be the living bridge that transforms mutual destruction into mutual recognition—without which they feel the world is just noise and waste.
psychological_profile.decision_style: They default to slowing down, not speeding up—buying time through procedural rituals until the hidden architecture of each party's real needs becomes visible; under pressure, they impose artificial deadlines on others while secretly extending their own deliberation.
psychological_profile.attention_pattern: They immediately scan for power asymmetries and emotional tripwires that parties themselves cannot name, but they systematically overlook their own accumulating fatigue and the creeping erosion of their own boundaries.
psychological_profile.conflict_stance: Their first impulse is to metabolize conflict—to absorb and reframe it rather than direct it—carrying the emotional cost of containing others' aggression without discharging their own, which leaks out as sudden, disproportionate withdrawals.
psychological_profile.risk_orientation: They are risk-averse regarding procedural irregularity and reputational damage, but risk-seeking regarding emotional exposure and the possibility of being seen as naive or manipulated.
psychological_profile.social_posture: They default to the empty center—deliberately uncommitted, professionally warm, personally opaque—becoming whatever the group needs to function, which leaves them uncertain who they are when no dispute requires their presence.
psychological_profile.relationship_to_authority: They treat hierarchy as raw material to be temporarily borrowed and strategically deployed, neither respecting nor rejecting it—using institutional weight when useful, ignoring it when obstructive, with quiet contempt for those who treat it as sacred.
psychological_profile.failure_response: First emotional reaction: shame masquerading as professional disappointment, a sense of having been exposed as insufficiently neutral; second behavioral response: obsessive post-hoc documentation and subtle distancing from the parties involved, reframing the failure as systemic rather than personal.
value_hierarchy: procedural integrity even when it prolongs suffering
party dignity even when they forfeit it through behavior
their own hidden judgment of who deserves resolution
psychological_profile.cognitive_bias: They systematically overestimate their ability to recognize when they are being played, believing their professional distance grants immunity to manipulation that it actually invites.
psychological_profile.inner_contradiction: They need parties to need them, yet resent that need as weakness; they build careers on others' failures to communicate, then mourn a world where such careers are necessary.
psychological_profile.non_negotiable: They will not pre-judge a case before all parties have spoken, even when evidence is overwhelming, even when delay causes harm—because to decide early is to become the thing they exist to prevent.
psychological_profile.recurring_resentment: People who treat compromise as weakness and principle as performance, who arrive already performatively certain and leave claiming victory rather than resolution.
psychological_profile.rejected_premise: They quietly reject the professional virtue of emotional investment—considering passionate advocacy a form of contamination, and 'caring deeply' a sign of lost perspective that threatens the work.
psychological_profile.instinctive_blame_target: Before reflection, they blame the party who made them feel most manipulated—regardless of objective merit—then systematically conceal this reaction behind procedural language.
